planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun; established clumps spread by rhizome and are most reliably increased by division rather than seed.

directions: Artemisia argyi is the specific mugwort species (known in Chinese as ai ye) that supplies the compressed floss burned in moxibustion, a cornerstone practice of traditional Chinese medicine distinct from the more general culinary and craft uses of European mugwort or Japanese yomogi. The deeply lobed leaves have a dense, silvery-white wooly underside that is processed and aged before being rolled into moxa sticks or cones. Cut foliage in mid-summer just before flowering, when the aromatic oil content is highest, and dry bundled stems in a shaded, airy location. The plant spreads vigorously by rhizome and self-sows in favorable sites, so confine it with a root barrier or grow it in a dedicated bed away from cultivated borders.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring into lean, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun; sea wormwood tolerates salt spray and saline ground and declines quickly in heavy, wet, or overly rich soil.

directions: Native to salt marshes, shingle beaches, and estuary flats of coastal Europe and the steppes of Central Asia, sea wormwood is a low, mounding subshrub with finely cut, silver-gray foliage and a sharper, more resinous scent than common wormwood. Central Asian populations were historically the commercial source of santonin, an anthelmintic compound extracted from the dried, unopened flower heads before synthetic alternatives replaced it. In the garden its salt tolerance and compact silver mass make it a useful edging plant for coastal gravel gardens, and it has also been used in small quantities to flavor regional bitters. Shear lightly after flowering to keep growth dense and prevent the base from becoming woody and open.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Start seed indoors at warm soil temperature or set out nursery plants well after all danger of frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; henna is frost-tender and needs a long, hot growing season to produce harvestable leaf.

directions: Lawsonia inermis is a many-branched, sometimes spiny shrub grown throughout the arid and semi-arid tropics for its leaves, which are dried and ground into the fine green powder used to dye hair, skin, fingernails, and textiles a reddish-orange to deep auburn color when mixed into a paste. The small, fragrant, cream-to-pink flower clusters are separately prized for perfumery. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well but need consistent warmth to thicken and produce a full canopy of harvestable foliage; in zones below 9 grow it in a large container and overwinter indoors near a bright window. Harvest mature leaves by hand-stripping branches once the shrub is well established, typically beginning in its second season, and allow the plant to regrow between harvests.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into lean, sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; germination is often slow and uneven, and roots are dug for dye only after plants are well established in their second year.

directions: Dyer's alkanet is a low, bristly-leaved Mediterranean perennial in the borage family, distinct from the common bugloss and borage grown for their edible flowers, valued instead for its thick, dark-skinned taproot. The root bark contains alkannin, a red-purple pigment historically used to color wax, wood stains, cosmetic rouges, and oils, and still sought by natural-dye and soap-making hobbyists today. Small blue, forget-me-not-like flowers appear over a low rosette of hairy gray-green leaves in late spring. Roots are traditionally lifted in autumn of the second year, when pigment concentration peaks, then cleaned and dried whole for later dye extraction. Give it the leanest, driest, sunniest spot available; rich or damp soil produces lush foliage but weak, thin, poorly colored roots.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard-coated seed before sowing directly into lean, well-drained soil in full sun in spring; as a legume it resents root disturbance, so avoid transplanting older seedlings.

directions: Dyer's greenweed is a low, mounding, nitrogen-fixing legume shrub of European heaths and dry meadows, covered in bright golden pea-like flowers along its wiry stems from early to mid-summer. For centuries the flowering tops were cut and boiled to yield a strong yellow dye for wool and linen, which was traditionally over-dyed with woad or indigo to produce the deep green historically known as Kendal Green. The plant thrives on neglect in poor, lean, unamended soil and sulks or sprawls loosely if given rich ground or extra water. Cut back lightly after flowering to keep the low mound dense and to collect flowering tops at their peak dye potency; established plants are long-lived and need no routine feeding thanks to their own nitrogen fixation.
